H1, H2 and the annual block are all present in the same sheet, and the annual block is the sum of the two halves. Summing all three would count every tonne twice. Filter to one period before aggregating: period equal to the compliance year is the annual figure.

pEPR reports a single Glass category while the recovery datasets split re-melt from other. A combined glass recycling rate is computable by summing the two recovery streams; a per-stream rate is not computable from these sources at all. Fibre Composite and Other have no recovery counterpart, so no rate can be computed for them either.

Small producers have no 2023 data: the obligation to report was phased in, so 2023 is large producers only. Small producer tonnage is in any case marginal, rising from 34,404 tonnes in 2024 to 82,326 in 2025 against 10.97 million for large producers in 2025, which is 0.7 per cent of the total. A 2023-to-2025 trend on the combined figure would therefore conflate real change with the phase-in.

The recyclability assessment exists for 2025 only, so there is no baseline to compare it against. It drives fee modulation from 2026, and the red-rated share varies enormously by material: wood 98.1 per cent, Other 94.2 per cent and flexible plastic 61.8 per cent against glass at 2.9 per cent and steel at 8.5 per cent. Flexible plastic is the substantial case, at 244,933 tonnes red-rated.

Packaging placed on the market by large producers fell from 12,146,078 tonnes in 2023 to 11,105,009 in 2024 and 10,970,502 in 2025, a 9.7 per cent decline over two years. Because each year was extracted on a different date, part of that movement may be reporting completeness rather than real change, and the 2023 figure is the stalest.

The regulator's recycling obligation estimate is derived from LARGE producer tonnage alone. Multiplying large producer supply by the 2026 target reproduces the published obligation exactly, to 0.00 per cent, for all seven materials; including small producers overshoots by 1.85 per cent for wood and is out for every other material. Small producers report their tonnage but carry no recycling obligation.

The 2026 statutory obligation totals 7,590,797 tonnes, derived as 2025 placed-on-market tonnage multiplied by the 2026 target for each material. The recovery datasets show the system already evidenced 7,795,720 tonnes of recycling in 2025, so the obligation sits about 2.6 per cent BELOW what was achieved the year before. The two figures use different material taxonomies and are only comparable in aggregate, but at aggregate level the 2026 targets do not require the system to recycle more than it already does. Plastic carries the lowest target at 57 per cent and steel the highest at 81 per cent.
